items.description: getEmailAssetsBucket() hardcoded the prod GCS bucket name and dropped the previous process.env.PUBLIC_ASSETS_BUCKET_NAME override, while its JSDoc still claimed to read from the env var. This meant dev/UAT digest drafts would embed image URLs pointing at the prod bucket.

The footer disclaimer rendered at a 2.52:1 contrast ratio (T.textVeryFaint on white), well under the WCAG AA 4.5:1 threshold for normal text. Product-decision styling/accessibility finding, marked Decided in the comment body.

weekStart was computed as new Date(Date.now() - 7d) at job-execution time rather than at dispatch/enqueue time. Because the processor runs with concurrency: 5, early- and late-executing jobs from the same fan-out could compute different week windows, causing the digest content window to drift by hours relative to the dispatch-time filter.

em.find(CrUserView, ...) in the dispatch processor had no limit on an unbounded, growing result set (all attorney/client pairs with recent messages), risking an OOM on the Cloud Run worker as feature usage grows.

items.acceptance_evidence: Not accepted; author declined on the review thread (identifiers redacted).
items.description: LLM-generated subject/body text flows into an attorney's Gmail draft without post-LLM validation, so a crafted client email in the COMMUNICATIONS context could attempt to steer the generated draft content (prompt injection), even though HTML/MIME-header injection itself is blocked by existing escaping.

createDraft() is the sole write surface of the whole client-digest feature (the call that actually creates the Gmail draft) yet had zero direct test coverage; the existing spec only exercised private __testing-exported helpers, not the public method.

The gmail-draft service spec tested through a private __testing export rather than the public createDraft surface, so createDraft could be deleted entirely and all four tests would still pass — a test backdoor that doesn't actually guard the shipped behavior.

items.acceptance_evidence: Not accepted; author declined on the review thread (identifiers redacted).
items.description: The dispatch processor's fan-out logic (flagByAttorney cache, null-attorney skip, per-pair feature-flag gating) had zero test coverage, so a bug that silently drops or duplicates an attorney/client pair would only surface in production on a Monday morning.

gmail-draft.service.ts threw InternalServerErrorException with a bare string message in two places, violating the project convention of always passing a structured object with message plus contextual identifiers, which hampers production debugging.

The weekly dispatch cron pattern ('0 14 * * 1') was hardcoded as a constant instead of read from env, unlike the rest of the feature's cron config — meaning any schedule change would require a code commit and redeploy.

formatFullName was independently duplicated in three files (plus similar clientHandle/toCommunications/toParticipant helpers) despite an existing shared getFullName utility with 11 other callers, violating the project's 'shared utils over privates' convention.

items.acceptance_evidence: Not accepted; author declined on the review thread (identifiers redacted). Commits referenced: 997c86fbda9.
items.description: findByUser is called with perPage: 1000 and orders messageAt DESC, so a high-volume client's older messages within the 7-day digest window are silently dropped from the LLM context with no detection or logging of the truncation.

MIME header construction inserted To:/From: addresses raw with no CRLF/control-char guard, and encodeMimeHeader only base64-encoded non-ASCII text, so an ASCII display name containing RFC 5322 special characters (e.g. a comma) would produce a malformed From: header.

The toCommunications filter (which drops entries with null senderEmail/senderPartyType and derives isFromAttorney from the STAFF enum) and the communications.length === 0 early-exit in processJob both had no test coverage.

The digest-content DTO spec had three gaps: no transformation guard on the happy path, an untested nextWeekItems.max(6) upper bound (asymmetric with the tested progressItems bound), and no extra-property rejection test for the nested .strict() ProgressItem/NeedsItem schemas.

The digest-template renderer spec never exercised the empty needsFromClient: [] state or an all-flagged:false digest — its fixture always included one flagged item and one needs item, leaving two render branches unverified.
Two new unit-test files used the .test.ts extension instead of the project's .spec.ts convention for unit tests (per .claude/rules/vitest.md and every sibling case-radar file).

items.description: DigestTemplateRendererService is a stateless @Injectable class wrapping a single render() call, diverging from the modal pattern used by all 9 sibling email templates (a plain exported factory function); the .renderer.tsx extension is also unique within services/.

*.types.ts files mixed three concerns — a runtime queue-name constant, a TypeScript JobData type, and an @Injectable() abstract DI-token class — violating the project's dot-separator convention that *.types.ts hold types only.

T.pageBg ('#e8e6e2') was documented as mirroring the --color-brown-50 design token, but the actual oklch value resolves to approximately #edebe7 — a visible ~2% darker drift, with an incorrect comment.

items.description: The hero combines width="600"/height="400" HTML attributes with a style={{ width: '100%', height: 'auto' }} CSS override; old Outlook's Word-based renderer ignores inline CSS on and uses the HTML attrs verbatim, so the image would overflow once the card narrows below 600px.
